learn.b: A C++ program is plain text in a .cpp file. The computer runs the code inside a function called main. When main finishes, the program ends. This tiny program prints one line of text.

Lines that start with # are instructions for the preprocessor, which runs before compiling. #include <iostream> copies in the code that lets you print and read. Without it the compiler does not know what cout is. Standard headers use angle brackets like <iostream>.

Every program needs exactly one main function. int means main gives back a whole number when it ends. Returning 0 tells the operating system that everything went fine. The code between the curly braces { } is the body of main.

Most statements end with a semicolon ;. A comment starts with // and the compiler ignores it. To run your code you compile it with a compiler such as g++, which makes an executable file, and then you run that file.

qs.why: The iostream header declares cout and cin.

qs.why: Execution always begins at main.

learn.b: cout prints to the screen. The << operator pushes values into it, and you can chain many of them. Text goes inside double quotes, numbers and variables do not.
learn.code: std::cout << "Score: " << 10 << "\n";

learn.b: To start a new line, print "\n" or std::endl. endl also flushes the output, which is a little slower, so \n is fine most of the time. Without either, everything prints on one line.
cin reads what the user types. The >> operator moves the typed value into a variable, and the variable must be declared first. cin stops reading at a space.

cout and cin live in the namespace std, so we write std::cout. You can write using namespace std; once near the top and then just write cout. Beginners often do this in small programs, but big projects keep std:: to avoid name clashes.
learn.code:
using namespace std;
cout << "Hi";

learn.b: A variable is a named box that holds a value. You write the type, the name, and usually a starting value. C++ is statically typed, so the type cannot change later.
int holds whole numbers. double holds decimal numbers. char holds one character in single quotes like 'A'. bool holds true or false. std::string holds text in double quotes.
A bool prints as 1 for true and 0 for false. A char prints as the character. Adding 1 to a char moves it along the alphabet, so 'A' plus 1 becomes 'B'.
learn.code:
bool done = false;
std::cout << done;   // 0

learn.b: Put const before a variable to stop it from changing. Names use letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, and are case sensitive. Always give a variable a starting value, because an uninitialized one holds garbage.
learn.code:

learn.b: Use + - * / for math and % for the remainder. Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, and brackets go first. The remainder operator only works on whole numbers.
When both numbers are int, / throws away the decimal part, so 7 / 2 is 3. Make one side a double to keep the decimals, as in 7 / 2.0, which gives 3.5.
x += 5 means x = x + 5. The same works for -=, *=, /= and %=. x++ adds one and x-- subtracts one.
Comparison operators are == != < > <= >= and give a bool. Use && for AND, || for OR and ! for NOT. A single = assigns a value, while == compares two values.
learn.code:
int age = 15;
bool teen = age >= 13 && age <= 19;

learn.b: An if statement runs code only when its condition is true. The condition goes in parentheses. Add else for the case when it is false, and else if for extra checks. Use curly braces for more than one line.
Conditions use ==, !=, <, >, <=, >= and can be joined with && and ||. Careful, = assigns and == compares. Only the first branch whose condition is true runs, and the rest are skipped.
switch picks a branch by comparing one whole number or char to several case values. After a matching case runs, you normally write break to stop. default runs when nothing matches.

If you forget break, execution continues into the next case, even if its value does not match. This is called fall-through. It is a common bug, but it is sometimes used on purpose to share code between cases.

qs.why: == compares, = assigns.

learn.b: A while loop repeats its body as long as the condition is true. The condition is checked before every round. Make sure something inside changes, or the loop never ends.
A for loop packs three parts in one line: a start, a condition and an update. It is perfect when you know how many times to repeat.
A do while loop runs the body first and checks the condition afterwards, so it always runs at least once. Note the semicolon after the closing while.
break leaves the loop immediately. continue skips the rest of the current round and jumps to the next one. You can put one loop inside another, which is called nesting.

learn.b: A function is a named block of code you can call many times. You write the return type, the name, the parameters in parentheses, and the body. return sends a value back to the caller.
If a function gives nothing back, its return type is void. It can still print things or do work. Calling it is just writing its name with arguments and a semicolon.

C++ reads top to bottom, so a function must be known before you call it. Either define it above main, or write a prototype, which is just the header with a semicolon. Then the full definition can come later.

By default the function receives a copy of each argument. Changing the parameter inside does not change the original variable in the caller. You can also give a parameter a default value, like int step = 1.

learn.b: An array holds a fixed number of values of the same type in a row. You write the type, the name and the size in square brackets. You can fill it with curly braces when you declare it.
The first element is a[0] and the last is a[n-1] for an array of size n. You read or change an element with square brackets. Looping with a for loop is the usual way to visit all elements.
If you give fewer values than the size, the rest become 0. So int a[5] = {1, 2, 3}; makes the last two elements 0. Without any braces the values are garbage, so always initialize.

sizeof(a) / sizeof(a[0]) gives the number of elements. C++ does not check bounds, so a[10] on a size 5 array reads memory that is not yours and causes bugs. Always keep the index between 0 and size minus 1.

learn.b: To work with text, include <string> and use std::string. It is a real type that grows and shrinks as needed. Join two strings with + and add to one with +=.
s.length() or s.size() gives the number of characters. s[0] is the first character, and indexes start at 0. You compare two strings with == and they match only if every character is equal.
s.substr(start, count) returns a piece of the string beginning at start with up to count characters. s.find("x") gives the position of the text, or a special value if it is missing.
learn.code:
std::string s = "banana";
std::cout << s.substr(1, 3);  // ana

learn.b: std::cin >> s stops at the first space. To read a whole line with spaces, use std::getline(std::cin, s). The first argument is the input stream and the second is the string to fill.

learn.b: std::vector is an array that can change size. Include <vector> and write the element type in angle brackets. It starts empty or with a list of values.

learn.b: v.push_back(x) adds x at the end. v.pop_back() removes the last element. v.size() gives how many elements there are, and v.empty() tells if there are none. v.back() is the last element.
learn.code:

learn.b: Use v[i] to read by index, starting at 0, just like an array. v.at(i) does the same but checks the index and throws an error if it is wrong. A range-based for loop visits every element without an index.

A vector knows its own size, grows when needed and cleans up after itself. Plain arrays have a fixed size and no safety. In modern C++ you reach for a vector first and only use arrays for simple fixed data.

learn.b: A reference is another name for an existing variable. You declare it with & after the type, and you must set it right away. After that, using the reference is exactly like using the original.
If a function parameter is a reference, the function works on the caller's variable instead of a copy. This lets a function change its arguments, like a swap function.
Copying a big string or vector is slow. Passing it as const std::string& avoids the copy, and const promises the function will not change it. This is the standard way to pass big read-only data.

A reference cannot be left empty and cannot be changed to refer to something else later. It is not a separate copy, so there is only one value in memory. Think of it as a nickname for the same variable.

learn.b: Every variable lives at an address in memory. The & operator in an expression gives the address of a variable. A pointer is a variable that stores an address, and it is declared with * after the type.
learn.code:
int x = 10;
int* p = &x;   // p holds the address of x

learn.b: Putting * in front of a pointer follows it to the value it points at. You can read the value or assign a new one, and the original variable changes too.
A pointer that points to nothing should be set to nullptr. Never dereference a null pointer, because the program will crash. Check with if (p != nullptr) before using a pointer you are unsure about.

Both let you reach another variable. A reference is simpler and safer and cannot be null. A pointer can be null and can be pointed at another variable later. You will need pointers for dynamic memory and for working with arrays in lower level code.
